name: JewelHuntrix costume-jewelry brand ruleset
description: Signal set for flagging valuable costume-jewelry brands from listing text and photos. Scores are indicative weights (0-100); require several positive signals to agree before flagging high-value. Confirm against SOLD comps, never asking prices.
notes: Brand names are corrected from the source video's auto-transcription (Monet not 'Monae'; Coro/Corocraft not 'Cororo').
A mark tells you what a piece claims to be; construction tells you what it is. Weight back-of-piece evidence highly.
'Style' / 'inspired by' / 'in the manner of' next to a brand name means NOT attributed - treat as red flag.

global_red_flags.effect: not attributed - lower score / manual review
quality downgrade (except brands where gluing is normal)
deprioritise for high-value flips - attribution lives on the back
possible reproduction (esp. Eisenberg/Trifari) - originals usually marked in mold

value_multipliers.note: often signals 1940s manufacture + intrinsic silver value
US costume jewelry: generally indicates post-1955

positive_signals: triple-plated / thick warm consistent plating with little discoloration
high-end clasp hardware (distinctive top lettering often mistaken for a karat stamp)
brand_red_flags: lightweight, warm-to-touch, or flaking plating (Monet plating is typically durable)

key_people: Alfred Philippe (fine-jewelry techniques: pavé, invisible settings)
marks: Trifari with crown over the T
positive_signals: fruit and floral motifs, enamel pieces
brand_red_flags: bare word 'Trifari' with NO crown, ©, or patent wording = forgery red flag
sterling piece with matte/frosted gold reverse can be a fake tell
'Boucher' jelly-belly = fake (Boucher didn't make Lucite jelly-bellies)

positive_signals: geometric shapes, sleek chains, bold simple forms
versatile pieces that suit modern wardrobes
brand_red_flags: gold plating quality is variable - grade each piece individually

positive_signals: figural work: floral and animal motifs (e.g. birds - highly collectible)
Coro Duette (matching double-clip set that fits into one frame)
brand_red_flags: plain 'Coro' basic-line mark = lower value than Corocraft/Pegasus

positive_signals: named designs (e.g. 'Fashion Flower', 'Golden Petals') - collectors value by name
thick durable substantial hardware with good click
brand_red_flags: mass-production focus: more wear on reverse; not prong-set = not premium tier
glued-in stones = NOT genuine Weiss (Weiss is always prong-set)

positive_signals: rare colors: electric blue, smoky gray, chartreuse (holy grail)
frosted lucite (often misidentified as frosted glass)
brand_red_flags: painted (not raised) veining or glued plastic = not genuine Lisner construction
missed tiny Dior stamp = under-attributed; verify magnified

marks: Miriam Haskell (marks vary by year: oval plaque, horseshoe, script tag)
construction_tells: flip over: visible wire work and NO glue
components feel artistic and layered, not mass-stamped
brand_red_flags: modern findings/bead types unavailable in the 1940s = reproduction

brands.display_name: Designer tier (Dior / Oscar de la Renta / Kenzo / YSL)

sub_brands.name: Christian Dior
sub_brands.note: Most common designer brand in thrift stores; never precious metal, so often overlooked. Watch the hyphenated 'CHR. DIOR' abbreviation - many sellers don't recognise it.

sub_brands.name: Oscar de la Renta
sub_brands.note: Ear-wrapping designs; commonly overlooked at yard/estate sales (no precious metal). Good resale.

sub_brands.name: Kenzo
sub_brands.note: Costume jewelry made 80s/90s/2000s; less commonly produced = value in brand name + scarcity. Plating can rub off / not highly polished, but still valuable. Try Google Lens.

sub_brands.name: YSL
sub_brands.note: Chunky designer looks; same collectors chase Dior clip-ons.

brand_red_flags: no precious-metal content means easy to overlook - that's the opportunity, not a downgrade
